sections.title: Example 3 — Inspect tables and delete one complete thread
sections.body: ```sql SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table'; SELECT thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, parent_checkpoint_id FROM checkpoints ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC LIMIT 10; ``` For ordinary state inspection, use `graph.get_state`; payload columns can be typed binary serialization rather than human-readable JSON. ```python saver.delete_thread("durable") assert saver.get_tuple(config("durable")) is None assert saver.get_tuple(config("review")) is not None ``` The lab confirms that deleting one thread leaves the other thread available. Do not delete only one checkpoint row and leave associated writes or dependency data behind. SQLite WAL mode improves reader/writer interaction, but SQLite still has write-contention limits. An async wrapper does not turn it into a distributed multi-writer service. One Python detail matters on Windows: `with sqlite3.connect(path)` commits or rolls back transactions but does **not** close the connection. Use `contextlib.closing` or explicit `close()` for your own inspection connections. The built-in saver's context manager closes its owned connection for you. **Run:** `python labs.py sqlite`. ### Run the three examples for this chapter The complete implementation is below. Numbered comments identify the three examples, and assertions check the behavior explained above. ```python def sqlite_examples(): with TemporaryDirectory() as tmp: path = str(Path(tmp) / "checkpoint.db") # 1. Close and reopen a file-backed saver. with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(path) as saver: graph = counter_graph(saver) graph.invoke({"count": 8}, config("durable")) with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(path) as saver: assert counter_graph(saver).get_state(config("durable")).values["count"] == 9 print("1. Reopened SQLite value: 9.") # 2. A human interrupt survives reconnecting and recompiling. with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(path) as saver: approval_graph(saver).invoke({"text": "Persist this review"}, config("review")) with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(path) as saver: result = approval_graph(saver).invoke(Command(resume={"approved": True}), config("review")) assert result["approved"] print("2. Pending review resumed after reopening the database.") # 3. Inspect raw tables, then use saver API for complete thread deletion. with closing(sqlite3.connect(path)) as conn: tables = {r[0] for r in conn.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'")} assert {"checkpoints", "writes"} <= tables print("3. Built-in tables:", sorted(tables)) with SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(path) as saver: saver.delete_thread("durable") assert saver.get_tuple(config("durable")) is None assert saver.get_tuple(config("review")) is not None ``` ```python sqlite_examples() ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
`PostgresSaver` and `AsyncPostgresSaver` come from the separate
`langgraph-checkpoint-postgres` package. In the inspected version, the constructor
accepts a connection/pool, optional pipeline, and serializer. It does **not** have
a generic `table_name=` or `schema=` argument.

The built-in migrations create this layout:

| Table | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `checkpoint_migrations` | Tracks applied library migrations |
| `checkpoints` | Checkpoint identity, parent link, runtime structure and metadata |
| `checkpoint_blobs` | Serialized channel values addressed by channel version |
| `checkpoint_writes` | Intermediate task outputs and control writes |

The blob table allows checkpoint records to reference channel versions rather
than treating every record as one independent JSON state document. A report that
reads only `checkpoints.checkpoint` can miss separately stored values. Use the
saver or graph APIs to reconstruct state.

sections.title: Example 1 — Use the standard built-in storage layout
sections.body:
```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver

with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(uri) as saver:
    saver.setup()
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
    graph.invoke({"count": 1}, config("pg-1"))
```

The recipe closes this connection and opens another. The new graph reads count
2. `setup()` initializes/migrates schema objects; run it in a controlled migration
step in production instead of allowing every request to compete over DDL.

When constructing your own psycopg connection, use the required compatible
settings, including `autocommit=True` and `row_factory=dict_row`. The migrations
include operations unsuitable for an ordinary open transaction. The official
[PostgreSQL saver instructions](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/libs/checkpoint-postgres/README.md)
explain this connection setup.

sections.title: Example 2 — Keep the built-in tables inside your agent_state schema
sections.body:
```python
from psycopg import Connection, sql
from psycopg.rows import dict_row

with Connection.connect(uri, autocommit=True, row_factory=dict_row,
                        prepare_threshold=0) as conn:
    schema = "agent_state"  # trusted deployment configuration
    conn.execute(sql.SQL("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS {}").format(sql.Identifier(schema)))
    conn.execute(sql.SQL("SET search_path TO {}").format(sql.Identifier(schema)))
    saver = PostgresSaver(conn)
    saver.setup()
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
    graph.invoke({"count": 5}, config("pg-schema-1"))
```

This creates `agent_state.checkpoints`, `agent_state.checkpoint_blobs`, and the
other library tables. It changes their database namespace, not their columns or
unqualified names. A schema-only search path avoids accidentally resolving a
missing table from `public` when the target schema is only partially initialized.

Every later connection must use the same search path. Configure it at connection
creation or through the database role's controlled settings. A `SET` executed
once on a random pooled connection does not configure every pool connection.

SQL values and identifiers require different treatment. Bind values using `%s`;
compose table/schema identifiers with `sql.Identifier`. Do not accept a schema
name from arbitrary HTTP JSON. Search paths also imply trust in the referenced
schemas; restrict who can create objects there. See
[PostgreSQL schema documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-schemas.html).

Inspect with:

```sql
SELECT current_schema(), current_setting('search_path');
SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'agent_state';
SELECT thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, metadata
FROM agent_state.checkpoints ORDER BY checkpoint_id DESC LIMIT 10;
```

sections.title: Example 3 — Share a pool across asynchronous requests
sections.body:
`database_recipes.py:postgres_pool` opens an `AsyncConnectionPool` with a fixed
`options='-c search_path=tutorial_agent_state'`. Every connection gets the intended
schema. It constructs `AsyncPostgresSaver(pool)`, compiles once, and uses
`await graph.aget_state` and `await graph.ainvoke`.

Create the pool at application startup; close it at shutdown after in-flight
tasks finish. Size the pool according to database capacity and workload. A pool
does not serialize two simultaneous runs on the same thread; use a per-thread
scheduling/locking policy at the application layer.

The sample uses a compatible Windows selector event-loop policy before starting
psycopg async work under Python 3.12. Review this platform requirement if changing
Python, psycopg, or the hosting environment.

sections.title: Run against your tutorial service
sections.body: **What this code covers** - 1. Standard built-in table layout. setup() performs versioned migrations. - 2. Your PostgreSQL schema, with the library's table names inside it. - Schema is trusted deployment configuration, never a raw request parameter. - A schema-only search path prevents falling back to existing public tables. - 3. Async application with a connection pool, using the same custom schema. - Windows psycopg async connections require a compatible selector event loop; - The __main__ block below configures it before asyncio.run(). - Configure os.environ["POSTGRES_URI"] in your environment first. **Defines:** `postgres()`, `postgres_pool()` ```powershell python -m pip install -r requirements-databases.txt $env:POSTGRES_URI = 'postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@HOST:5432/TUTORIAL_DATABASE' python database_recipes.py postgres ``` Replace placeholders and use your environment's TLS settings. The script creates a fixed `tutorial_agent_state` schema and unique tutorial thread IDs. It does not delete that schema afterward. The three service examples were API-checked but not executed against a PostgreSQL server during author validation. ### Complete database implementation, inline The next cell defines all three service-dependent examples. The following cell leaves them disabled by default. Configure the connection environment variable and enable only the backend you intend to run. Live service connections were not tested when preparing this notebook. ```python def postgres(): from psycopg import Connection, sql from psycopg.rows import dict_row from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver uri = os.environ["POSTGRES_URI"] thread = "tutorial-pg-" + uuid4().hex c = config(thread) # 1. Standard built-in table layout. setup() performs versioned migrations. with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(uri) as saver: saver.setup() # tutorial convenience; a production deployment job owns this assert counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 1}, c)["count"] == 2 with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(uri) as saver: assert counter_graph(saver).get_state(c).values["count"] == 2 print("1. Built-in Postgres reconnect passed.") # 2. Your PostgreSQL schema, with the library's table names inside it. # schema is trusted deployment configuration, never a raw request parameter. schema = "tutorial_agent_state" with Connection.connect(uri, autocommit=True, row_factory=dict_row, prepare_threshold=0) as conn: conn.execute(sql.SQL("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS {}").format(sql.Identifier(schema))) # A schema-only search path prevents falling back to existing public tables. conn.execute(sql.SQL("SET search_path TO {}").format(sql.Identifier(schema))) saver = PostgresSaver(conn) saver.setup() assert counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 5}, c)["count"] == 6 assert conn.execute("SELECT current_schema() AS name").fetchone()["name"] == schema rows = conn.execute( "SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=%s", (schema,), ).fetchall() assert {"checkpoints", "checkpoint_blobs", "checkpoint_writes", "checkpoint_migrations"} <= { row["table_name"] for row in rows} print("2. Custom PostgreSQL schema contains the built-in table layout.") # 3. Async application with a connection pool, using the same custom schema. with asyncio.Runner(loop_factory=asyncio.SelectorEventLoop) as runner: runner.run(postgres_pool(uri, schema, c)) async def postgres_pool(uri, schema, c): from psycopg.rows import dict_row from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres.aio import AsyncPostgresSaver # Windows psycopg async connections require a compatible selector event loop; # the __main__ block below configures it before asyncio.run(). async with AsyncConnectionPool( conninfo=uri, min_size=1, max_size=4, open=False, kwargs={"autocommit": True, "row_factory": dict_row, "prepare_threshold": 0, "options": f"-c search_path={schema}"}, # trusted static schema above ) as pool: await pool.wait() saver = AsyncPostgresSaver(pool) graph = counter_graph(saver) assert (await graph.aget_state(c)).values["count"] == 6 assert (await graph.ainvoke({"count": 9}, c, durability="sync"))["count"] == 10 print("3. Async pool loaded and continued the custom-schema thread.") ``` ```python RUN_POSTGRES_EXAMPLES = False # Configure os.environ["POSTGRES_URI"] in your environment first. if RUN_POSTGRES_EXAMPLES: await asyncio.to_thread(postgres) else: print("postgres: optional live-service examples skipped.") ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The `langgraph-checkpoint-mongodb` integration exposes explicit database and
collection name arguments. That makes name customization different from the
PostgreSQL built-in saver. The document fields inside those collections still
belong to the integration's storage contract.

sections.title: Example 1 — Store order checkpoints in your own collections
sections.body:
```python
from pymongo import MongoClient
from langgraph.checkpoint.mongodb import MongoDBSaver

with MongoClient(uri) as client:
    saver = MongoDBSaver(
        client,
        db_name="tutorial_agent_state",
        checkpoint_collection_name="order_snapshots",
        writes_collection_name="order_task_writes",
    )
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
    graph.invoke({"count": 10}, config("mongo-1"))
```

The final count is 11. The saver manages separate checkpoint and pending-write
collections. Naming the first collection `order_snapshots` does not mean each
document is shaped like your `orders` business document. Keep operational order
records in their own collection, and link them with application IDs.

The supported constructor and identifier requirements are documented in the
[MongoDBSaver reference](https://langchain-mongodb.readthedocs.io/en/latest/langgraph_checkpoint_mongodb/saver/langgraph.checkpoint.mongodb.saver.MongoDBSaver.html).

sections.title: Example 2 — Reconnect and inspect indexes
sections.body:
Create a new `MongoClient`, the same saver configuration, and a graph with the
same code. Reading thread `mongo-1` should yield count 11. Reading from another
database or a different pair of collections produces a different storage space.

```python
indexes = client["tutorial_agent_state"]["order_snapshots"].index_information()
print(indexes)
```

Check the actual installed schema's compound indexes for checkpoint identity and
task-write uniqueness. If you point the saver at pre-existing collections, do
not assume the constructor has repaired every unsuitable index or validation
rule. Inspect and migrate those collections deliberately.

Prefer state values small enough for the database's document limits. Put large
documents in appropriate object/document storage and keep stable references in
the graph. Query state through `graph.get_state` rather than assuming all fields
are directly readable BSON values with your original Python types.

sections.title: Example 3 — Give disposable conversations a one-hour TTL
sections.body:
```python
saver = MongoDBSaver(
    client,
    db_name="tutorial_agent_state",
    checkpoint_collection_name="ephemeral_snapshots",
    writes_collection_name="ephemeral_writes",
    ttl=3600,
)
```

This integration's TTL is expressed in **seconds**. The recipe uses fresh
ephemeral collections and checks the generated `expireAfterSeconds` index.
It does not wait an hour or claim precise deletion timing. MongoDB TTL deletion
is performed asynchronously by the server; expiration is not an exact scheduler.
See [MongoDB TTL indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/index-ttl/).

If an approval may remain pending for a week, a one-hour TTL is unsuitable.
Choose retention around the longest supported resume window and the backend's
dependency requirements. Do not apply arbitrary expiry to ancestor data needed
to reconstruct retained checkpoints, especially when using delta channels.

sections.title: Run the three recipes
sections.body: ```powershell $env:MONGODB_URI = 'mongodb://HOST:27017' python database_recipes.py mongodb ``` Use authenticated/TLS settings for your service. Collection creation and demo writes happen only when this script runs. Live database behavior is not part of the locally executed validation report. ### Complete database implementation, inline The next cell defines all three service-dependent examples. The following cell leaves them disabled by default. Configure the connection environment variable and enable only the backend you intend to run. Live service connections were not tested when preparing this notebook. ```python def mongodb(): from pymongo import MongoClient from langgraph.checkpoint.mongodb import MongoDBSaver uri = os.environ["MONGODB_URI"] c = config("tutorial-mongo-" + uuid4().hex) # 1. Application-selected database and collection names. with MongoClient(uri) as client: saver = MongoDBSaver(client, db_name="tutorial_agent_state", checkpoint_collection_name="order_snapshots", writes_collection_name="order_task_writes") assert counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 10}, c)["count"] == 11 # 2. New client and saver read the same saved conversation. with MongoClient(uri) as client: saver = MongoDBSaver(client, db_name="tutorial_agent_state", checkpoint_collection_name="order_snapshots", writes_collection_name="order_task_writes") assert counter_graph(saver).get_state(c).values["count"] == 11 indexes = client["tutorial_agent_state"]["order_snapshots"].index_information() assert indexes print("1-2. Custom collections, reconnect and index inspection passed.") # 3. Separate ephemeral collections with a one-hour TTL (SECONDS). ttl_saver = MongoDBSaver(client, db_name="tutorial_agent_state", checkpoint_collection_name="ephemeral_snapshots", writes_collection_name="ephemeral_writes", ttl=3600) counter_graph(ttl_saver).invoke({"count": 3}, config("ephemeral-" + uuid4().hex)) ttl_indexes = client["tutorial_agent_state"]["ephemeral_snapshots"].index_information() assert any(v.get("expireAfterSeconds") == 3600 for v in ttl_indexes.values()) print("3. TTL index configured; expiry timing is not tested by this script.") ``` ```python RUN_MONGODB_EXAMPLES = False # Configure os.environ["MONGODB_URI"] in your environment first. if RUN_MONGODB_EXAMPLES: mongodb() else: print("mongodb: optional live-service examples skipped.") ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Redis persistence is a combination of the saver format and the Redis service's
own durability/eviction configuration. A saver does not enable disk persistence
or replication on your behalf. The integration requires Redis JSON and search
capabilities; a plain older Redis deployment without these capabilities is not
enough. See the [Redis integration project](https://github.com/redis-developer/langgraph-redis).

sections.title: Example 1 — Keep full checkpoint history
sections.body:
```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.redis import RedisSaver

with RedisSaver.from_conn_string(uri) as saver:
    saver.setup()
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
    graph.invoke({"count": 2}, config("redis-1"))
```

The recipe closes and reconnects, then verifies count 3. `setup()` establishes
the search indexes used by the integration. Your Redis deployment needs
appropriate persistence, replication and eviction choices if losing a thread
would be unacceptable. Reconnecting to a running service proves client-lifetime
independence; it does not prove recovery after losing the Redis host.

sections.title: Example 2 — Customize key prefixes and expire inactive data
sections.body:
```python
with RedisSaver.from_conn_string(
    uri,
    checkpoint_prefix="tutorial_orders_cp",
    checkpoint_write_prefix="tutorial_orders_writes",
    ttl={"default_ttl": 60, "refresh_on_read": True},
) as saver:
    saver.setup()
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
```

These prefix parameters were verified in installed version 0.5.2. They configure
the saver's keys; they are not user authentication and are not a PostgreSQL-style
schema. Inspect the associated search-index names and prefixes before using
multiple saver configurations on a shared production Redis instance. Separate
services are a clearer isolation boundary where independent ownership is needed.

Redis integration TTL is in **minutes**, unlike the MongoDB recipe's seconds.
`refresh_on_read=True` extends expiry on supported reads. A client polling thread
state can therefore keep it alive. Decide whether you want inactivity expiry or
an absolute business deadline; they are different policies.

The runnable recipe demonstrates construction and a graph call. It does not
claim to have tested expiry timing or isolated index ownership on a live server.

sections.title: Example 3 — Keep only the latest checkpoint with a shallow saver
sections.body:
```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.redis.shallow import ShallowRedisSaver
```

The third recipe uses a shallow saver with a fresh prefix and thread. This is
useful when current resumable state matters but retaining a complete history is
unnecessary. Do not select shallow retention and then build a UI that assumes
all historical checkpoints remain available for replay and forks.

“Shallow” describes retention behavior. It is not a way to make arbitrary expiry
or database eviction safe. Validate the exact backend's support for your channel
types, pending-work recovery, and lifecycle operations.

sections.title: Run
sections.body: ```powershell $env:REDIS_URI = 'redis://HOST:6379' python database_recipes.py redis ``` Use your service's TLS/authentication URI and a dedicated tutorial instance. Async applications can use the integration's `AsyncRedisSaver` and its async setup/lifecycle APIs. Do not mix synchronous database calls into an async request handler without considering blocking behavior. ### Complete database implementation, inline The next cell defines all three service-dependent examples. The following cell leaves them disabled by default. Configure the connection environment variable and enable only the backend you intend to run. Live service connections were not tested when preparing this notebook. ```python def redis(): from langgraph.checkpoint.redis import RedisSaver from langgraph.checkpoint.redis.shallow import ShallowRedisSaver uri = os.environ["REDIS_URI"] c = config("tutorial-redis-" + uuid4().hex) # 1. Full history and reconnect. Requires RedisJSON and Search capabilities. with RedisSaver.from_conn_string(uri) as saver: saver.setup() assert counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 2}, c)["count"] == 3 with RedisSaver.from_conn_string(uri) as saver: saver.setup() assert counter_graph(saver).get_state(c).values["count"] == 3 print("1. Redis full-history reconnect passed.") # 2. Application-controlled key prefixes and TTL (MINUTES, not seconds). with RedisSaver.from_conn_string( uri, checkpoint_prefix="tutorial_orders_cp", checkpoint_write_prefix="tutorial_orders_writes", ttl={"default_ttl": 60, "refresh_on_read": True}, ) as saver: saver.setup() assert counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 4}, config("ttl-" + uuid4().hex))["count"] == 5 print("2. Custom key prefixes and TTL example completed.") # 3. Shallow retention: use a separate demo prefix and a fresh thread. with ShallowRedisSaver.from_conn_string( uri, checkpoint_prefix="tutorial_shallow_cp", checkpoint_write_prefix="tutorial_shallow_writes", ) as saver: saver.setup() assert counter_graph(saver).invoke({"count": 6}, config("shallow-" + uuid4().hex))["count"] == 7 print("3. Shallow saver completed; this is not a full time-travel archive.") ``` ```python RUN_REDIS_EXAMPLES = False # Configure os.environ["REDIS_URI"] in your environment first. if RUN_REDIS_EXAMPLES: redis() else: print("redis: optional live-service examples skipped.") ```

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Read [custom_sqlite.py](checkpointers_masterclass/custom_sqlite.py) alongside this chapter. It is a
complete runnable teaching saver for the ordinary channels used in this course.
It implements the synchronous persistence methods and asynchronous thread
adapters. Its limitations are explicit: no DeltaChannel reconstruction, pruning,
thread-copy implementation, distributed lock, or native async database driver.

sections.title: The interface and what each method must preserve
sections.body:
| Method | Input / output responsibility | Common broken implementation |
|---|---|---|
| `put` | Save full checkpoint and metadata; return exact new config | Stores only `messages` or loses parent ID |
| `get_tuple` | Exact checkpoint or latest in thread/namespace; include pending writes | Returns raw JSON instead of CheckpointTuple |
| `list` | Ordered history, namespace filtering, metadata filters, before/limit | Returns an unordered collection or ignores filters |
| `put_writes` | Save task outputs with task identity, write index and ordering path | Ignores writes and reruns successful parallel work |
| `delete_thread` | Remove all namespaces and associated rows for one thread | Deletes only the root checkpoint row |
| Async counterparts | Same semantics through async interfaces | Blocks the event loop or returns a coroutine where an iterator is required |
| `get_next_version` | Monotonically advancing compatible channel versions | Uses random values that do not order consistently |

The sample inherits the base integer version generator. It stores complete
checkpoint payloads, so `new_versions` does not drive separate blob writes. A
backend using version-addressed blobs must use that argument appropriately.
Consult the [checkpoint API reference](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/checkpoints/)
when changing the pinned dependency versions.

sections.title: Example 1 — Choose your table names and payload columns
sections.body:
```python
with CustomSqliteSaver("orders.db", prefix="orders") as saver:
    graph = counter_graph(saver)
    graph.invoke({"count": 5}, config("order-flow-1"))
```

This creates `orders_snapshots` and `orders_task_writes`. The constructor validates
the prefix as a short identifier. All thread IDs and other data are bound SQL
parameters. A table identifier cannot be passed as an ordinary `?` value.

The snapshot table's primary key is:

```text
(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id)
```

Its payload contains the entire runtime checkpoint serialized as `(type, bytes)`.
Metadata has a separate typed payload. `parent_checkpoint_id` makes the lineage
explicit. A root checkpoint has no parent. The returned config identifies the
new record, not its parent.

Why two typed columns per payload? Bytes alone do not tell the deserializer
which encoding to use. Why a namespace in the key? Parent and child graph state
must not collide. Why not just use `thread_id` as the primary key? That would
overwrite history and break replay/fork expectations.

sections.title: Example 2 — Preserve task writes and prove recovery
sections.body:
The pending-write table's primary key is:

```text
(thread_id, checkpoint_ns, checkpoint_id, task_id, write_index)
```

`task_path` is stored separately and participates in ordering. Normal retry
duplicates use conflict handling that retains the existing task write. Reserved
control channels use the pinned library's reserved write indexes and its batch
replacement policy. The implementation uses `WRITES_IDX_MAP` rather than
inventing indexes that might collide with ordinary outputs.

`get_tuple` loads writes in `(task_path, task_id, write_index)` order and returns
`(task_id, channel, decoded_value)` tuples. The task path is not interchangeable
with task ID. Deterministic write ordering matters for order-sensitive reducers.

The custom lab runs the same good/flaky parallel graph as the built-in saver.
The successful task runs once and the failed task twice. An automated test also
checks ordinary duplicate writes, reserved error updates, and path ordering.

Writes and checkpoints can be scheduled independently. The sample deliberately
does not add an immediate foreign key that would reject a valid write because
the referenced checkpoint row has not arrived yet. This is a design choice to
review before translating the schema to another database.

sections.title: Example 3 — History filters, async access and complete deletion
sections.body:
`list` can enumerate all namespaces if namespace is omitted, or only the root
when it is explicitly `''`. `before` uses the runtime-generated ordered checkpoint
ID. Metadata filtering occurs before limiting results. The teaching version
filters metadata in Python; large histories need indexed, carefully allowlisted
queries and bounded retrieval.

The asynchronous methods use `asyncio.to_thread`, a shared connection configured
for cross-thread access, and a lock. This keeps SQLite calls off the event loop
but serializes database work within this saver. It is not a throughput upgrade.
`alist` materializes results before yielding; do not copy that approach for an
unbounded production history scan.

`delete_thread` deletes writes and snapshots in one local transaction. The test
suite injects a failure into the second delete and verifies that the first delete
rolls back. It also verifies that other threads survive and all namespaces of
the deleted thread disappear.
